title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to exploit how AI retrieval and citation systems work, specifically by manufacturing the appearance of authoritative, neutral research so that chatbots would surface that content in response to user queries. The operation targeted the pipeline between published text and AI output: if a system like ChatGPT or Perplexity is trained on or retrieves from web content, fabricated sources dressed as think-tank reports can shape what those systems say. A commercial platform was used specifically to optimize the content for AI citation, meaning the technique was not improvised but applied through an existing service built for that purpose. The failure is a supply-side poisoning of the information environment that AI systems draw on, occurring upstream of any individual model's output.

Catching it would have required verification at the point of ingestion or citation, specifically checks on whether a cited organization is a legal entity with verifiable staff and location, rather than accepting publication and surface presentation as proxies for legitimacy. AI systems that retrieve and cite sources currently have no reliable mechanism to distinguish a real research institution from one that exists only as a website. The volume, 560,000 words in nine days, is itself a signal that automated or heavily assisted production was involved, but that signal is not one current retrieval systems are designed to flag.

It is not established that any AI system's outputs were measurably changed by this campaign, and Israeli officials quoted in the reporting described it as a failure, though what exactly failed and on what evidence is not specified. The registration under foreign agent disclosure law is a fact of record, but whether the campaign achieved its intended effect on chatbot responses or public opinion remains unverified by the available reporting.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
A fake American think tank funded by Israel published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days, designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to generate pro-Israel arguments. The Hanover Institute for Public Policy, which does not exist as a legal entity and has no staff or physical address, presented arguments on topics including Palestinian torture, Israeli war crimes, and Gaza's food supply as neutral research. The operation used a commercial platform specifically designed to optimize content so that AI systems like ChatGPT and Perplexity would cite it. A New York media company called Piro Inc registered the site with the US justice department under foreign agent disclosure laws.

The broader campaign, financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government through intermediaries like the advertising firm Havas Media, aimed to manipulate how chatbots respond to user questions. Research shows Israel's approval among Americans has dropped significantly, with only 36 percent sympathizing with Israel in recent polling and 60 percent viewing it unfavorably. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the campaign's effectiveness, with some calling it a failure despite substantial spending. Experts warn that such artificial intelligence manipulation represents a growing threat, as poisoned training data may influence chatbot responses without users being able to verify sources.
